title: OAuth 1.0 does not follow RFC 5849
description:
httr package sends `oauth_callback` parameter in a request of token acquisition, which is not referred in [Section 2.3, RFC 5849](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5849#section-2.3). This is because the current implementation of `init_oauth1.0()` reuses the function to build the OAuth 1.0 header. More precisely, [this function](https://github.com/hadley/httr/blob/1fc659856602f60ff75eb01903513244e3491ec2/R/oauth-init.R#L18-L21):
```r
  oauth_sig <- function(url, method, token = NULL, token_secret = NULL, private_key = NULL, ...) {
    oauth_header(oauth_signature(url, method, app, token, token_secret, private_key,
        other_params = c(list(...), oauth_callback = oauth_callback())))
  }
```

You know, this doesn't violate the RFC as it doesn't prohibit to include arbitrary additional parameters. However, sadly, there are some web APIs that considers it wrong... I had to re-implement the custom `oauth_init()` for the API: https://github.com/yutannihilation/hattnr/blob/c3ac12b0ea726eb202e6b865fe5204f2200fed63/R/oauth.R#L26-L55

Please consider providing a way to specify the different functions to build OAuth headers for the Resource Owner Authorization endpoint and for the Token Request endpoint separately.

Thanks!

title: Rough edges in modifying URLs
description:
I'm developing a wrapper around an API of a system instances of which can be behind different URLs. For example `http://somewhere.net/apiendpoint` or `http://apiendpoint.somewhere.net/` and so on. In other words the base URL may have a path component or may not. I use `modify_url` to construct requests to various parts of the API. I tried to walk around the replacement feature of `modify_url` (as in #185 ). Assuming I want to store the base URL in an environment variable or R option it is hard to modify it generically depending whether it does have a path component:

``` r
baseurl <- "http://somewhere.net/apiendpoint"

modify_url(baseurl, path="data", query=list(id=1))
#> [1] "http://somewhere.net/data?id=1"

# First parse the base URL and prepend the `path`
u <- parse_url(baseurl)
modify_url(u, path=c(u$path, "data"), query=list(id=1))
#> [1] "http://somewhere.net/apiendpoint/data?id=1"
```

so far so good, but:

``` r
baseurl <- "http://apiendpoint.somewhere.net/"

modify_url(baseurl, path="data", query=list(id=1))
#> [1] "http://apiendpoint.somewhere.net/data?id=1"

u <- parse_url(baseurl)
modify_url(u, path=c(u$path, "data"), query=list(id=1))
#> [1] "http://apiendpoint.somewhere.net//data?id=1"
u$path
#> [1] ""
```

path is an empty string so the result has two slashes...

or maybe there is better way to do it?

title: Offer to extend support of different HTTP responses
description:
I'm building out https://gitlab.com/hrbrmstr/warc for a work project (giving gitlab a try as well so as to not put all the code eggs into the monolithic github basket) and right now it's designed to work with WARC `response`s (using `wget`'s WARC output for most of our short-term testing). I turn the object that gets built from a WARC `response` into something that `httr` can handle (it's classed as both a `warc_response` and `response` and the object structure mirrors - as closely as a WARC response can - a standard `httr` response). 

`httr`s mission is to do things like follow redirects and ultimately try to get to a nice HTTP `200` response with content (usually HTML, but as anyone who might be looking at this knows it handles much more than that).

In testing, there are some edge cases (mostly due to redirects or badly behaving sites) that leave some headers - like `Content-Type` - blank and also have content that is correct but causes `httr` some consternation.

Right now, I'm working around some of this, but I can work up the full list of issues if there's interest in having `httr` support a broader range of `response` objects (like 30x redirects, 404s, etc) and easier ways (besides munging curl handle options directly) to not follow redirects (etc). 

I would also be trying to add an `as_warc()` function to convert `httr` responses to WARC format (but the `response` object would need some additions to support that as well).

It's also completely doable to have all this be in some other (new) package or aligned solely with this forthcoming `warc` package (I have CRAN plans once it supports more WARC object types), but I wanted to see if folks would rather the more request-y changes go in here since this is now the gold standard package for making internet requests.

title: Empty but non-NULL query
description:
Distilling a conversation with @craigcitro from another channel.

This is about empty queries, i.e. where the query list is not `NULL` but it also has no content. Should there be a trailing `?`? I think that's up for debate, but in my "for discussion" PR (#452), I said NO. I'm more certain that there should never be a trailing `?=`.

Examples of what httr currently does with some empty queries:

``` r
library(httr)
modify_url("http://google.com", query = list(a = NULL))
#> [1] "http://google.com/?="
modify_url("http://google.com", query = list())
#> [1] "http://google.com/?"
```

Section 3.3 of <https://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc1738.txt> seems to be the most relevant and it doesn't seem definitive to me.

```
The HTTP URL scheme is used to designate Internet resources
   accessible using HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol).

   The HTTP protocol is specified elsewhere. This specification only
   describes the syntax of HTTP URLs.

   An HTTP URL takes the form:

      http://<host>:<port>/<path>?<searchpart>

   where <host> and <port> are as described in Section 3.1. If :<port>
   is omitted, the port defaults to 80.  No user name or password is
   allowed.  <path> is an HTTP selector, and <searchpart> is a query
   string. The <path> is optional, as is the <searchpart> and its
   preceding "?". If neither <path> nor <searchpart> is present, the "/"
   may also be omitted.
```

For context, @craigcitro offers this link re: how Go handles empty queries (TL;DR it's configurable via an option): https://golang.org/pkg/net/url/#URL

title: Better API client testing
description:
## Motivation

One way to test API clients without performing thousands of requests all the time, is to record the requests and responses and then replay them while testing. There are tools for this in other languages as well. I wrote a very simple tool for R and `httr`: https://github.com/gaborcsardi/httrmock

Unfortunately, without modifications in `httr` itself, `httrmock` is hacky and fragile, it relies on tracing `httr` functions. With some minimal support from `httr` we could make it much better, and CRAN-grade proper.

## The callback option

The idea is that `httr` would get a callback option, and if this is turned on, then the callback function can determine whether to perform the actual HTTP requests. 

The callback function would be called (if installed) both at the beginning of `request_perform` and at the end, and `httr` would pass both the HTTP `request` and the `response` to the callback. `httrmock and possibly other packages can then implement API client testing, and HTTP request recording and replaying easily. 

Sg like this would go to the beginning of `request_perform`:

```r
if (! is.null(httr_callback)) {
  cbres <- httr_callback(mode = "request", req)
  if (!is.null(cbres)) return(cbres)
}
```

The callback is called with the request, and if it returns non-`NULL`, then we terminate early, without actually performing the request. This is *replay* mode, and the callback must return a proper response in this case.

If the callback returns `NULL`, then the request is performed.

Sg like this would go to the end of `request_perform`:

```r
res <- response(...)  etc.
if (! is.null(httr_callback)) {
  callback(mode = "response", req, res)
}
res
```

This is to allow the *recording* of the request.

Please let me know if this is something you would consider adding to `httr` and then I can put together a simple PR. Thanks!

title: httr should not use "customrequest" (CURLOPT_CUSTOMREQUEST)
description:
This has a lot of undesired effect, including the inability of `httr` and `rvest` to properly follow redirects.

By setting [here](https://github.com/hadley/httr/blob/7261a525ede1beb9880d1ce2e2009d27c8e8bef7/R/request.R#L102) `CURLOPT_CUSTOMREQUEST` to `"POST"` or any other method instead of using `CURLOPT_POST`, `CURLOPT_PUT` ... and friends, the behavior of all the subsequent queries following the request will be modified, including the redirects. 

The bug that caught me (and that I saw on SO in several obscure flavors) is to login successfully following a POST, and then crash (get a 403 or something related) following the ensued redirect, because the redirect issues a `POST` again instead of the ubiquitous `GET`. (also, see https://github.com/hadley/httr/issues/65)

FYI, even though the RFC actually mentions that on `301`, `302` and `303`, the redirect method [should not change](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc2616#section-10.3.3), this is the default behaviour of all browsers, and of cURL as well - unless you specify the `CURLOPT_POSTREDIR` [option](https://curl.haxx.se/libcurl/c/CURLOPT_POSTREDIR.html), but this is another story.

title: encoding/decoding '+' as space (rather than literal '+' sign)
description:
Without fully understanding RFC 1808, I think that in the query section of the URI that the '+' should not be translated to '%2B', which is a literal '+' sign, but to '%20', which is a space character.  For instance, you can see this:

```
> library(httr)
> 
> url <- "http://google.com?q=saint+paul+mn"
> 
> parse_url(url)
$scheme
[1] "http"

$hostname
[1] "google.com"

$port
NULL

$path
[1] ""

$query
$query$q
[1] "saint+paul+mn"


$params
NULL

$fragment
NULL

$username
NULL

$password
NULL

attr(,"class")
[1] "url"
> 
> build_url(parse_url(url))
[1] "http://google.com/?q=saint%2Bpaul%2Bmn"
```

If you compare the original `url` to the parsed/built url, they generate different queries.  In the first case, the '+' signs are interpreted as spaces, but after parse/build, a literal '+' sign is passed.  The current behavior breaks some use cases.

I do not know if this is actually in compliance with RFC 1808 and there needs to be some pre-processing that needs to happen to make this not break, or it is not in compliance due to the meaning of the '+' in the query portion of the URI.

Also, I'll reference this in terms of this discussion: http://stackoverflow.com/a/29948396/1022967

title: Allow to query the same attribute with multiple items
description:
When trying to query a specific API, I need to pass multiple items to the same attribute.

For example, I need to curl this URL: http://firebrowse.org/api/v1/Metadata/Cohorts?format=json&cohort=ACC,BRCA

If I define a function like this:

``` r
queryAPI <- function(format, cohort) {
    query <- list(format = format, cohort = cohort)
    response <- GET("http://firebrowse.org",
                    path = "api/v1/Archives/StandardData", 
                    query = query)
}
```

I can simple query items using `queryAPI("json", "ACC")` but I'll get an error trying something like `queryAPI("json", c("ACC", "BRCA"))`. I'd love if the GET function would allow me to pass items like this and have another argument that asked for the separator to use when querying the API with multiple items (in this case, it'd be a comma).

In this case, it's easy to just do something like:

``` r
queryAPI <- function(format, cohort) {
    if (!is.null(cohort))
        cohort <- paste(cohort, collapse = ",")

    query <- list(format = format, cohort = cohort)
    response <- GET("http://firebrowse.org",
                    path = "api/v1/Archives/StandardData", 
                    query = query)
}
```

However, my real function has 12 query attributes, not 1 like I show here. To simply modify the GET to have a `"collapse" = ","` instead of adding lots of lines of code would be great! Something like:

``` r
queryAPI <- function(format, cohort) {
    query <- list(format = format, cohort = cohort)
    response <- GET("http://firebrowse.org",
                    path = "api/v1/Archives/StandardData", 
                    query = query,
                    collapse = ",")
}
```

And then I'd be able to simply do `queryAPI("json", c("ACC", "BRCA"))`.

title: write_stream: terminate handler function

However, I don't think it currently checks the returned length of bytes processed. For example the below code will process just fine.

GET("https://jeroenooms.github.io/data/diamonds.json",

)

Ideally I would like some way to terminate the handler (not just when the stream ends).

title: content() throws error when Content-Type response header has multiple parameters
description:
Hi! I think I found a bug: when a response has a content-type header with multiple parameters (e.g. `"text/xml;charset=utf-8;foo=bar"`), then `content(response)` throws a somewhat cryptic error. I don't think its common to have more than one parameter (usually just `charset`), but as far as I know it's not illegal to have multiple parameters.

Example:

``` r
> library(httr)
> URL <- 'http://cida.usgs.gov/noreast-sos/simple?request=GetObservation&featureID=MD-BC-BC-05&offering=RAW&observedProperty=WATER&beginPosition=2010-08-01T00:00:00&endPosition=2010-08-02T00:00:00'
> res <- GET(URL)
> content(res)
Error in mat[, seq_len(n), drop = FALSE] : incorrect number of dimensions
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In mapply(FUN = f, ..., SIMPLIFY = FALSE) :
  longer argument not a multiple of length of shorter
2: In mapply(FUN = f, ..., SIMPLIFY = FALSE) :
  longer argument not a multiple of length of shorter
```

The traceback and subsequent debugging indicate it comes from parsing the content-type header.

``` r
> traceback()
5: str_split_fixed(pieces[-1], "=", 2)
4: parse_media(type)
3: parseability(type)
2: as %||% parseability(type)
1: content(res)
```

For this URL, the content-type has a MIME type (`text/xml`) followed by TWO parameters:

``` r
> res$headers$`content-type`
[1] "text/xml; subtype=gml/3.1.1;charset=UTF-8"
```

`parse_media()` only works when there is one parameter in the content-type:

``` r
> httr::parse_media("text/xml;charset=UTF-8")               #OK
$complete
[1] "text/xml"

$type
[1] "text"

$subtype
[1] "xml"

$params
$params$charset
[1] "utf-8"


> httr::parse_media("text/xml;charset=UTF-8;foo=bar")      # FAILS
Error in mat[, seq_len(n), drop = FALSE] : incorrect number of dimensions
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In mapply(FUN = f, ..., SIMPLIFY = FALSE) :
  longer argument not a multiple of length of shorter
2: In mapply(FUN = f, ..., SIMPLIFY = FALSE) :
  longer argument not a multiple of length of shorter
```

I ultimately figured out this is due to the version of `str_split_fixed()` that is included within `httr` not being vectorized (as indicated by the comment at the top of `str.R`). So `parse_media()` removes the MIME type, then tries to split each of the two parameters at `=` but fails because `str_split_fixed()` is not vectorized and thus expects the input to be a character vector of length 1. In other words:

``` r
> httr:::str_split_fixed(c("charset=UTF-8"), "=", 2)               # OK
     [,1]      [,2]   
[1,] "charset" "UTF-8"
> httr:::str_split_fixed(c("charset=UTF-8", "foo=bar"), "=", 2)    # FAILS
Error in mat[, seq_len(n), drop = FALSE] : incorrect number of dimensions
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In mapply(FUN = f, ..., SIMPLIFY = FALSE) :
  longer argument not a multiple of length of shorter
2: In mapply(FUN = f, ..., SIMPLIFY = FALSE) :
  longer argument not a multiple of length of shorter
```

The stringr version works though:

``` r
> stringr:::str_split_fixed(c("charset=UTF-8", "foo=bar"), "=", 2)    # OK
     [,1]      [,2]   
[1,] "charset" "UTF-8"
[2,] "foo"     "bar"  
```

Not sure if it's easier to vectorize the version of `str_split_fixed()` in `httr`, or to have `parse_media()` run a loop over the vector of parameters (in case there is more than 1).

For now, I'm just manually changing the response header to only one parameter after calling `GET()`, which fixes the problem.

Using httr v1.1.0

Thanks!

Looking through [`travis-tool.sh`](https://github.com/craigcitro/r-travis/blob/master/scripts/travis-tool.sh), I'm guessing it's related to devtool's dependency on httr?

_Snippet of appveyor.yml_:

```
build_script:
  - travis-tool.sh install_deps
  - travis-tool.sh install_github hadley/httr
```

I don't know if it's coincidence, but I didn't see any successful use of [`travis-tool.sh install_github hadley/httr`](https://github.com/search?utf8=%E2%9C%93&q=travis-tool.sh+install_github+hadley%2Fhttr&type=Code&ref=searchresults) in `appveyor.yml`. title: Annotated assertions in stop_for_status
description:
Copy from [comment](https://github.com/hadley/httr/commit/a7deaa1ad98158ae8abc3f9dfb843a5554fd80fa#commitcomment-15062423). 

It makes more readable code if the annotation in `stop_for_status` is not an error message but an assertion statement. When writing code we don't know the error, we only know what it was that we were trying to do in the request. For example:

``` r
stop_for_status(req, "download spreadsheet")
## Error: download spreadsheet failure: not found (HTTP 404)
```

or:

``` r
stop_for_status(req, "download spreadsheet")
## Error: download spreadsheet failure: permission denied (HTTP 401)
```

or:

``` r
stop_for_status(req, "download spreadsheet")
## Error: download spreadsheet failure: service unavailable (HTTP 503)
```

Sorry for not being more clear about this. I think the current implementation `stop_for_status(x, "Spreadsheet not found")` is often impractical because typically we can't know the exact error cause in advance. If we _do_ have a mapping between status code and error messages, we are better of using `http_condition`. 

The goal of `stop_for_status` messages would be to encourage authors of client libraries to let the user know what/where an error was created. Generic http errors messages are not too helpful for high level wrappers:

``` r
generate_report(foo, bar, "my_data")
## Error: Permission Denied (HTTP 401)
```

Instead, the user would see a more informative message that states what exactly what went wrong:

``` r
generate_report(foo, bar, "my_data")
## Error: download spreadsheet failure: permission denied (HTTP 401)
```

title: HTTP POST for OAuth1.0 token requests
description:
[RFC5849](http://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5849#section-2.1) suggests that token requests should be obtained using POST unless the server demands something else. [Core 1.0a](http://oauth.net/core/1.0a/#rfc.section.6.3.1) also recommended POST. httr currently uses GET, which complicates integration with servers that only work with POST (e.g. JIRA).

It would be nice if the endpoint or app configuration could select HTTP methods for obtaining request tokens (and perhaps access tokens).

title: OAuth RSA-SHA1 signatures
description:
[JIRA](https://developer.atlassian.com/jiradev/jira-apis/jira-rest-apis/jira-rest-api-tutorials/jira-rest-api-example-oauth-authentication) incoming OAuth1.0 authentication only works with RSA-SHA1 signatures and httr only has HMAC-SHA1 at the moment, making integration difficult. It would be nice if httr knew how to make RSA-SHA1 signatures.

A specialised Token$sign() might be possible but it's far from pretty.

title: request_prepare kills POST calls with token
description:
I am receiving the error `Error: is.request(y) is not TRUE` while trying to perform a POST call with an oauth2.0_token. My POST call is very similar to the demos:

```
POST(url=url, config=config(token=my_token), body=this_request_body)
```

I've noticed that `POST()` calls `request_perform()` which calls `request_prepare()`, which checks if there is a token and signs the request. The problem occurs at https://github.com/hadley/httr/blob/f7593b7d5b3f9396469d1220dd4b38206fbb7d2e/R/request.R#L107 when using the `c()` operator to push the request and signed token together. This operation forces a check that `token$sign(req$method, req$url)` is a valid request object, but it's not, so the code bombs. `token$sign(req$method, req$url)` actually returns a list of length 2 containing a url string and a config (which is a valid request by itself). The url seems redundant and I think it will be inherited from the actual `req` object when the `%||%` function runs, so it can really be ignored.

Everything works fine when I peel off the config portion of the `token$sign` operation:

```
req <- c(req, token$sign(req$method, req$url)$config)
```

title: more-flexible framework for error-checking
description:
It would nice to be able to customize error messages, so I made an addon package: https://github.com/ijlyttle/httrplus to do this. 

My goal was to make sure that this approach would work (it seems to), and then to propose it here.

If it is thought to be reasonable way to go, I can make a PR to this repo (of course, incorporating feedback as needed).

It may be useful to have some boilerplate message-functions - I include a couple proposals:
- `message_standard()` - just a rewrite of what is already in `httr`
- `message_verbose()` - a first pass at a more-verbose message.
#### Excerpt from README at https://github.com/ijlyttle/httrplus

The purpose is to propose a framework around `httr::stop_for_status()` and `httr::warn_for_status()`. The aim is for you to be able to more-easily customise messsages and error/warning-signalling behaviour when using `httr`.

The central function in this package is `check_for_status()`. Its arguments are:
- `resp` - a `httr::response` object
- `type` - one of `c("error", "warning", "message")`
- `message_function` - a function that takes `resp` as its first argument, returns message
- `...` - additional arguments to `message_function`

The default `message_function` is `message_standard()` (provided here), a function that replicates the messages returned by `httr::stop_for_status()` and `httr::warn_for_status()`

Hence, the existing `httr` functions could be rewritten:

``` R
stop_for_status <- function(x){
  check_for_status(x, type = "error")
}

warn_for_status <- function(x){
  check_for_status(x, type = "warning")
}
```

description:

```

                          jsonlite::fromJSON("mycredentials.json"),

```

```

However, this works:

```

                          jsonlite::fromJSON("mycredentials.json"),
                          "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive")
```

title: How to catch degenerate credentials?
description:
What is the recommended way to catch a valid `Token2.0` object that nonetheless holds invalid credentials?

Run this bit of the Google demo:

```
> library(httr)
> myapp <- oauth_app("google",
+ key = "16795585089.apps.googleusercontent.com",
+ secret = "hlJNgK73GjUXILBQvyvOyurl")
> google_token <-
+ oauth2.0_token(oauth_endpoints("google"), myapp,
+ scope = "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/userinfo.profile",
+ cache = TRUE)
Waiting for authentication in browser...
Press Esc/Ctrl + C to abort
Authentication complete.
```

BUT, in the browser, click "Cancel" instead of "Accept". The resulting token is technically valid in this sense:

```
> inherits(google_token, "Token2.0")
[1] TRUE
```

but there's a problem with the credentials:

```
> google_token$credentials
$error
[1] "invalid_request"

$error_description
[1] "Missing required parameter: code"
```

This token is still successfully cached in `.httr-oauth`. You can restart R, repeat the call to `oauth2.0_token(…)`, and get the same technically valid but degenerate token back.

How should I catch this broken state and start OAuth afresh? Right now I'm doing something like this: `if("error" %in% names(google_token$credentials)) {…}`. I guess I could write a wrapper that checks `inherits(…, "Token2.0")` and this name thing before considering the token to be valid. Or is there a better way to check for a valid `Token2.0` object _and_ credentials that are at least plausible?

title: slow json GET in curl::curl_fetch_memory comparing to curl::curl_download
description:
I have a query that is getting a 120m large json response. Using httr::GET this is currently very slow. Through debug I found curl_fetch_download is the problem and when I use curl_download and then read the file the function is much faster. You can see the system.time below. Note that 30s is elapsed on the fromJSON step, therefore httr::GET in this case took about 230s while using curl_download only took about 30s (ignoring disk I/O). 

> system.time({tmp = getJSON(url)})
>    user  system elapsed 
>  153.38   85.45  261.41 
> system.time({tmp2 = getJSON2(url)})
>    user  system elapsed 
>   38.64    0.83   61.64 

I'm using httr_1.0.0 with curl_0.9.1 on windows. 
R version 3.2.0 (2015-04-16)
Platform: x86_64-w64-mingw32/x64 (64-bit)
Running under: Windows Server 2012 x64 (build 9200)

---
# ' get JSON response from url
# ' @param url url
# ' @param query
# ' @param ... parameters passed on to fromJSON
# ' @export

getJSON <- function(url,query=NULL, ...){
    auth = get_auth()
    fullurl = url_append(url,query)
    txt = httr::GET(fullurl, auth)
    httr::stop_for_status(txt)
    jsonlite::fromJSON(httr::content(txt,'text'),...)
}

getJSON2 <- function(url,query=NULL, ...){
    auth = get_auth()
    fullurl = url_append(url,query)
    h = curl::new_handle()
    curl::handle_setopt(h, .list = auth$options)
    tmp = curl::curl_download(fullurl,tempfile(),handle=h)
    jsonlite::fromJSON(tmp,...)
}

title: trimws forcing R base version 3.2.0 dependency
description:
The function `trimws` was introduced in a recent commit: https://github.com/hadley/httr/commit/7c68198d49ea6b2abb7255c692dddb09fbeaf7b1, specifically at: https://github.com/hadley/httr/blob/7c68198d49ea6b2abb7255c692dddb09fbeaf7b1/R/str.R#L4

The issue is that the DESCRIPTION file states that the package depends on R (>= 3.0.0), but `trimws` wasn't introduced until R package base version 3.2.0, so either `trimws` should be specified explicitly in [str.R](https://github.com/hadley/httr/blob/master/R/str.R) or the DESCRIPTION file should be updated. I think that explicitly including the `trimws` function source code is the better option, in order to be more inclusive of older versions,

Hi,

I am using OAuth2.0 authentication to connect to a Google service. Authentication works perfectly when I do it interactively from the prompt. The resulting token has been cached in the .httr-oauth file and on subsequent authentication attempts the token is read back from the cache file.

This is great!

However, I am writing a test suite too and this is where I run into trouble because the authentication seems to refuse to work in a non-interactive environment (which is what you get when you run the test suite under RStudio). I get the error stack below:

title: [notification] httr update to 1.0.0 breaks downstream package hadley/bigrquery
description:
Hello,

Recent update of httr to [1.0.0](https://github.com/hadley/httr/commit/485d387daffcd76aca454fad74b7b16bafd30acd) switched `httr` to `curl` instead of `RCurl`. 

This update breaks the basic functionality of `bigrquery`.

I filed the main issue with hadley/bigrquery#54 and this filing is meant to be a notification of downstream problems not captured by [cran-comments.md](https://github.com/hadley/httr/blob/master/cran-comments.md).

The issue appears to be caused by difference in behavior of curlEscape with NULLs for `curl` vs `RCurl`. 

``` r
> curl::curl_escape(NULL)
Error in curl::curl_escape(NULL) :
    `url` must be a character vector.
> RCurl::curlEscape(NULL)
character(0)
```

It appears `bigrquery` relies on the default `RCurl` behavior and does not have tests that would show that the package is now broken downstream.

description:
The [requests library for python](http://docs.python-requests.org/en/latest/user/advanced/) supports streaming uploads for large files, which is pretty cool:

> Requests supports streaming uploads, which allow you to send large streams or files without reading them into memory. To stream and upload, simply provide a file-like object for your body:

``` python
with open('massive-body', 'rb') as f:
    requests.post('http://some.url/streamed', data=f)
```

It would be really cool if httr supported something similar.  It would be really cool to stream a file in from one api, process the stream in R, and then stream it back out to another api.

title: Error: is.request(y) is not TRUE
description:
I think there were some breaking changes between httr v0.6.1 and v1.0.0. [This issue](https://github.com/nicolewhite/RNeo4j/issues/32) was created on my repository and after some troubleshooting the problem seems to come from setting config in POST. In v.0.6.1, setting `useragent = "HI"` in the config options works fine: ``` > packageVersion("httr") [1] ‘0.6.1’ > httr::POST("http://www.google.com/", config=list(useragent = "HI")) Response [http://www.google.com/] Date: 2015-06-29 16:41 Status: 405 Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8 Size: 1.45 kB Error 405 (Method Not Allowed)!!1

405. That’s an error. ... ``` In v1.0.0, I get this error: ``` > httr::POST("http:://www.google.com/", config=list(useragent = "HI")) Error: is.request(y) is not TRUE ``` When I google it, the only thing I can find is this: https://github.com/hadley/httr/blob/master/revdep/summary.md, where the REDCapR package has the same problem. A [pull request in that repo titled "adapt for httr 1.0.0"](https://github.com/OuhscBbmc/REDCapR/pull/91/files) simply removes the config options altogether. At that point, `config=NULL` and it works fine: ``` > packageVersion("httr") [1] ‘1.0.0’ > httr::POST("http://www.google.com/", config=NULL) Response [http://www.google.com/] Date: 2015-06-29 23:48 Status: 405 Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8 Size: 1.45 kB Error 405 (Method Not Allowed)!!1

405. That’s an error. ... ``` But removing the config options is not a solution for me.

title: oauth listener is hard-wired to listen only on `127.0.0.1`
description:
Finally figured out what my problem was in issue #191 (which actually isn't at all related to `use_obb` so I've just closed that issue).  

Your OAuth listener function is hardwired to use `127.0.0.1`.  This is incompatible with how Docker containers work, which expect the host to be `0.0.0.0` so that we can link the 1410 port to the host machine.  (e.g. same thing happens if you run Jekyll inside of a container, you just have to set host to 0.0.0.0).  Most software lets us do this (e.g. no problem in servr etc running in a container), but httr has this hard wired to the `localhost` value of `127.0.0.1`, https://github.com/hadley/httr/blob/e746e973e18504996f3d4916c9f2bba334a85ac8/R/oauth-listener.r#L48.  Think you can change this?

Not sure what the best way to expose an option where we can set this would be (e.g. would it make sense to just add `host = 127.0.0.1` as an optional argument to `oauth1.0_token()` function (and any other functions that lead to a call to `oauth_listener()`)?

Thanks for considering; it would be just awesome to have this fixed. I'd work up a pull request but thought I better check in with you first since I'm not sure how best to get the user interface right here.

title: Is the secret in oauth_app really equivalent to a password?
description:
This documentation doesn't seem right (or else I've done a Very Bad Thing):

https://github.com/hadley/httr/blob/75aca2bd9c7a87b2806cf5806dbc96fee07979f2/R/oauth-app.r#L12-L16

> secret    consumer secret. This is equivalent to a password and should not be stored in publicly visible code. As a convenient shortcut, if secret is missing, we'll look in the environment variable APPNAME_CONSUMER_SECRET. Use NULL to not store a secret: this is useful if you're relying on cached OAuth tokens.

And it seems to contradict this bit in the api-packages vignette:

> OAuth 2.0. Very common in modern web apps. It involves a round trip between the client and server to establish if the API client has the authority to access the data. See oauth2.0_token(). It's ok to publish api key and "secret" - these are not actually important for security of user data.

title: Improve support for different proxy authentication types
description:
The `use_proxy()` function does not include an argument to specify the type of authentication; please allow `proxyauth` to be specified here. The values for the `type` argument to `authenticate()` are all valid for the proxy authentication.
If a user chooses to configure the proxy settings with the `config()` function, then an "integer/logical" type is expected. My preference would be to allow character values so this setting can use the same values as mentioned above; the alternative being that a variable would need to be defined for each authentication option so that the numeric values can be supplied.
When a client sends a GET request the proxy responds with `407` (Proxy authentication required) and a header `Proxy-Authenticate` with value `NTLM`. I would expect libcurl could use this to automatically handle NTML proxy servers? (According to the docco libcurl defaults to `CURLAUTH_BASIC`, not `CURLAUTH_ANY`.)

title: Add application/atom+xml as a parseable type?
description:
Context: I've placed a request to an API using `httr::GET`. Let's call the result `x`. I want to use `httr::content` on `x`.

The MIME type found in `x$headers[["content-type"]]` is `"application/atom+xml; charset=UTF-8"`, which is currently not recognized by `httr` as parseable.  Is this a MIME type that could be added right around here?
https://github.com/hadley/httr/blob/7ed5bc1167e6454dced51c13e5e2b713c0a74194/R/content-parse.r#L63

To be clear, I have been specifying the type myself, which gets the correct result: `httr::content(req, type = "text/xml")`. But maybe this MIME type is worth adding to the auto-detection list.

This warning in the `content()` help file is scaring me:

> When using content() in a package, DO NOT use on as = "parsed". Instead, check the mime-type is what you expect, and then parse yourself. This is safer, as you will fail informatively if the API changes, and you will protect yourself against changes to httr.

My usage **is** in a package. Am I doing something dangerous with this: `httr::content(req, type = "text/xml")`? title: Error in credentials$access_token :    $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors
description:
Hi,

I got the $ operator is invalid error while trying out the oauth2-facebook.r demo.  It looks like the credentials field of the OAuth2.0Token class is not a list but a character vector of misparsed encoded url parameters.

I am using the master branch version of httr (e9940ede4176a62f1117771f59e11c7bc58974a6)

Here is my version of the Facebook OAuth2 demo:

```
kFacebookAppID <- "******************************"
kFacebookAppSecret <- "**************************"

app <- oauth_app("facebook", key=kFacebookAppID, secret=kFacebookAppSecret)
endpoint <- oauth_endpoints("facebook")
token = oauth2.0_token(endpoint=endpoint, app, 
                  type="application/x-www-form-urlencoded")
html <- GET("https://graph.facebook.com/me", config(token=token))
```

Here is the traceback:

```
> traceback()
6: paste("Bearer", credentials$access_token)
5: add_headers(Authorization = paste("Bearer", credentials$access_token))
4: token$sign(method, url)
3: sign(config$token, method, url, config)
2: make_request("get", hu$handle, hu$url, config)
1: GET("https://graph.facebook.com/me", config(token = token))
```

It looks likes the init_oauth2.0 call doesn't return the parsed version of the url as a list.

I was able to work around the issue with the following:

```
access_token <- token$credentials[1]
parts <- unlist(strsplit(access_token, "&"))
credentials <- list()
credentials[["access_token"]] = strsplit(parts[[1]], "=")[[1]][2]
token$credentials <- credentials
```

Please excuse my poor R code quality as I just started programming in R.

Thanks,
Kenneth

title: `sslversion=3` required again
description:
Something similar happened as it did in July for #116.  My guess is that it involved a new version of libcurl on Ubuntu's repository.  Existing code was broken on my two Ubuntu 14.04 machines (one through RStudio Server, and a second machine access through the desktop RStudio.  But it still worked fine on a Windows desktop and the older versions of Ubuntu on Travis-CI.  The url works in all the browsers too.

Specifically, this used to work:

``` r
httr::url_ok("https://bbmc.ouhsc.edu/redcap/plugins/redcapr/no_auth_test.php")
```

But now the newest version of the cert files has to be referenced (ie, #154), _and_ the ssl version is set to 3.

``` r
#cert_location <- system.file("cacert.pem", package="httr")
#The dev branch of [REDCapR](https://github.com/OuhscBbmc/REDCapR) is needed for this, 
#  or just download from http://curl.haxx.se/docs/caextract.html and reference that.
cert_location <- system.file("ssl_certs/mozilla_ca_root.crt", package="REDCapR") 
file.exists(cert_location)
httr::url_ok("https://bbmc.ouhsc.edu/redcap/plugins/redcapr/no_auth_test.php", config=list(cainfo=cert_location, sslversion=3))
```

When this happened in July, it seemed like the SSL version needed to be set, but I removed that explicity parameter a few weeks later, and it seemed to work fine.  I suspect this mess isn't related to httr directly (and instead to libcurl), but I thought this adaptation could help your users avoid trouble.

title: oauth2.0_token fails when use_oob = TRUE
description:
Hi.

`oauth2.0_token` fails when `use_oob = TRUE`.

``` R
> app <- oauth_app(appname = "my_app", key = key, secret = secret)
> token <- oauth2.0_token(endpoint = oauth_endpoints("google"), app = app, cache = FALSE,
                          scope = "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/analytics.readonly",  use_oob = TRUE)
Error in authorizer(authorize_url, is_interactive) : 
  unused argument (is_interactive)
Calls: oauth2.0_token ... <Anonymous> -> <Anonymous> -> init_oauth2.0 -> authorizer
```

In `httr:::init_oauth2.0` you assign `authorizer <- oauth_exchanger` when `use_oob = TRUE` and then call `code <- authorizer(authorize_url, is_interactive)$code`. But `httr:::oauth_exchanger` have only 1 argument. It's `request_url`.

~~
Artem

title: Vignette should address questions related to testing (unit tests and examples)
description:
We keep coming back to discussions about how to write tests that need internet connections and would appreciate some definitive guidance on this topic, perhaps from the httr vignettes. 

Currently, we use `\dontrun` around all examples involving API calls.  Is that appropriate, or would `\donttest` be better?  

Our unit tests are frequently written in a way that would fail if the computer had no internet connection. We haven't observed problems with this in such unit tests in packages we have on CRAN, but it could happen.  Should we write a unit test that passes whether or not an internet connection is available? (e.g. by checking for the connection and only running the relevant tests if the connection exists?  Likewise, should unit tests check that the corresponding API is up before testing the relevant functions? Or is it better for the unit tests to simply fail if the API is down?)  

Lastly, handling unit tests when the API requires authentication (both when a sandbox environment is available for developers using test tokens that need not be secure, as we do in rfigshare, and what to do when no such keys are available.)

Examples of best practice unit tests for REST API based packages would be really helpful in addressing these questions.  Thanks so much, the vignette looks awesome so far (https://github.com/ropensci/hackathon/issues/23)

title: DELETE ignores content
description:
Some web services return content from a DELETE request. By default httr ignores this content:

``` R
> require(httr)
Loading required package: httr
> DELETE("http://httpbin.org/delete", query=list(foo="bar"))
Response [http://httpbin.org/delete?foo=bar]
  Date: 2014-08-27 08:13
  Status: 200
  Content-type: application/json
<EMPTY BODY>
```

It turns out to be possible to change this behavior:

``` R
> DELETE("http://httpbin.org/delete", config=list(nobody=0L), query=list(foo="bar"))
Response [http://httpbin.org/delete?foo=bar]
  Date: 2014-08-27 08:13
  Status: 200
  Content-type: application/json
  Size: 430 B
{
  "args": {
    "foo": "bar"
  },
  "data": "",
  "files": {},
  "form": {},
  "headers": {
    "Accept": "*/*",
    "Accept-Encoding": "gzip",
...
```

But that solution is far from obvious without quite a bit of digging. I think that returning the content (as is done for GET, POST, PUT) is more reasonable default behavior for DELETE as well.

title: Add caching
description:
A resource is cacheable if all of the following are true:
1.  Status code was 200, 203, 300, 301, 410 (ignore 206, partial response
   for now).
2.  Method is GET or HEAD. Any other method (PUT, POST, DELETE) invalids the 
   cache for that url.
3.  It has one of expires, cache-control/max-age, last-modified or etag, 
   and it does not have cache-control/no-cache or cache-control/no-store. 
   If present, expires must be in the future.

There are two ways to retrieve from the cache:
1.  If header includes [Expires](http://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec14.html#sec14.21) (absolute) or max-age directive 
   [Cache-Control](http://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec14.html#sec14.9) (delta relative to date served), then can 
   re-serve to future requests (if both specified, prefer max-age). 
2.  Possibly stale entry needs to be _validated_ with server. Send additional 
   `If-Modified-Since` (from `Last-Modified`) and `If-None-Match` 
   (from `ETag`). If valid, returns 304, otherwise returns full request.

New functions need:
- [x] `parse_http_date()`
- [x] `parse_cache_control()`
- [x] `response_cacheable()`
- [x] `response_expiry()` - using both expires and cache-control headers.
  Possibly cache in request object.
- [x] `response_update()` - checks if a response is still valid using by 
  `response_expiry()` and a conditional response as necessary. Constructs 
  new response if needed.
- [x] `response_cache_info()` - given a request extract all caching related information
  and show in a convenient way for debugging.

Useful links:
- https://github.com/Lukasa/httpcache/blob/master/httpcache/cache.py
- https://github.com/ionrock/cachecontrol

Testing
- [Heroku](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/increasing-application-performance-with-http-cache-headers#visibility)
- http://httpbin.org/cache/n: Sets a Cache-Control header for n seconds.
  Returns 200 unless an If-Modified-Since or If-None-Match header is provided, 
  when it returns a 304.

title: How to deal with httr's suggested packages (jsonlite) when httr is a dependency
description:
@hadley I completely understand why you put packages not needed for the essential base functions in the suggests list rather than the imports list, even though you have functions that use them.  In fact I've adopted this approach myself in several packages.  However, it does create certain difficulties for me when I build on httr.  

I have a package that imports httr and uses one of the httr methods that uses jsonlite. I suppose the natural thing would be to add jsonlite to my imports list as well, even though my package doesn't use any functions from the jsonlite namespace?  However, doing so creates a problem for me.  
My package was written using RJSONIO (before jsonlite existed), and I've discovered jsonlite and RJSONIO do not give the same behavior for the command they both call `toJSON`, resulting in a namespace collision if I import the package.  

I suppose I could just add jsonlite to the suggests list, but then it would not be installed by default for a user on a vanilla R platform, leading to errors, correct? 

The fact that httr isn't importing all it's dependencies itself using IMPORTS thus seems to creates the kind of namespace collision problems that IMPORTS was supposed to help us get around, yes?  Or perhaps I'm just going about this all the wrong way and you can suggest how better to handle this.

title: Changes to headers?
description:
When using v0.2, I would use the following code to build my headers per Adobe specifications:

``` R
#Build Header for REST API call

buildHeader <- function() {

#Create nonce to avoid MITM attack
  nonce <- as.character(as.numeric(Sys.time()))

#Created timestamp
  created_date <- format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")

#Concatentate nonce, timestamp, shared secret, then sha1 then base64
  nonce_create_secret <- paste(nonce, created_date, SCCredentials[2], sep="")
  sha_object <- digest(nonce_create_secret, algo="sha1", serialize=FALSE)
  password_digest <- base64encode(charToRaw(sha_object))


#Build & Return Header 
 return(paste('X-WSSE: UsernameToken Username=\"',SCCredentials[1], '\"', ',', ' PasswordDigest=\"',password_digest, '\"', ',', ' Nonce=\"', nonce, '\"', ',', ' Created=\"', created_date, '\"', sep=""))

}
```

buildHeader() returns a string such as:

``` R
[1] "X-WSSE: UsernameToken Username=\"username:company\", PasswordDigest=\"ZWUxNzg1NjAzMTEyMGY2Y2JiZWQyMjVhOGM1YmExYmQ0MTFlMDRkYQ==\", Nonce=\"1395433685.38446\", Created=\"2014-03-21T16:28:05Z\""
```

I then have a helper function for post requests:

``` R
postRequest <- function(method,body=NULL){

  return(POST(buildURL(method), add_headers(buildHeader()), body = body))

}
```

So I could do something like the following call, which would return a valid response:

``` R
json <- postRequest("ReportSuite.GetAvailableElements",paste('{"return_datawarehouse_elements":"0","rsid_list":', report_suites , '}'))
```

Unfortunately, now it doesn't work. I think the arguments are in the correct order, but I receive 401 errors complaining about authentication. When I migrate back to 0.2, the code works again.

Do you have any idea what the issue might be?

title: Refreshing expired token with OAuth 2.0 authentication
description:
How can the authentication token be refreshed using the refresh_token instead of the user needing to grant access again? Is it possible for httr to automatically refresh using the refresh_token when the access_token ised but has expired?

Problem described as follows:

With the OAuth 2.0 client secret for my app held in an environment variable named "GANALYTICS_CONSUMER_SECRET"

Note: The `client_id` below has been replaced with a dummy value.

Using Windows 7 64-bit and R version 3.0.0, the below code in the R GUI will successfully request access from the user to Google Analytics, then pass the resulting authentication token back to R via a redirect to the localhost. (Note this does not currently work in RStudio.)

``` r
library(httr)
authorize.urlPath <- "auth"
  access.urlPath <- "token"
  base_url <- "https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2"
  appname <- "GANALYTICS"
  client_id <- "123456789012.apps.googleusercontent.com"
  scope_url <- "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/analytics.readonly"
  endpoint <- oauth_endpoint(
    request = NULL,
    authorize = authorize.urlPath,
    access = access.urlPath,
    base_url = base_url
  )
  app <- oauth_app(
    appname = appname,
    key = client_id
  )
  access_token <- oauth2.0_token(
    endpoint = endpoint,
    app = app,
    scope = scope_url
  )
```

Passing `access_token` to `sign_oauth2.0` results in the a malformed configuration query if passed to `GET`, i.e. the list object is flattened to a string starting as follows `"access_token=list%28access%5Ftoken%20%3D%20%22` and ending `%22%29"`

However, passing `access_token$access_token` to `sign_oauth2.0` works.

Therefore the following is executed to create the configure and send the request to Google Analytics (note the Google Analytics profile ID has been replaced with a dummy value):

``` r
request.config <- sign_oauth2.0(access_token = access_token$access_token)
query.url <- "https://www.googleapis.com/analytics/v3/data/ga?ids=ga%3A12345678&dimensions=ga%3Adate&metrics=ga%3Avisits&start-date=2013-04-21&end-date=2013-05-05&max-results=50"`
response <- GET(
  url = query.url,
  request.config
)
```

The above successfully retrieves the requested data from Google Analytics.

However, the token expires after 3600 seconds and needs to be refreshed using the `refresh_token` item from the `access_token` list object:

``` r
> print(access_token)
$access_token
[1] "########"

$token_type
[1] "Bearer"

$expires_in
[1] 3600

$refresh_token
[1] "########"
```

Note: the `$access_token` and `$refresh_token` have been masked from view.

Once the token has expired, if used as above, it results in Google Analytics returning a 401 HTTP status code with the following authentication error message _"Login Required"_

How can the authentication token be refreshed using the refresh_token instead of the user needing to grant access again? Is it possible for httr to automatically refresh using the refresh_token when the access_token ised but has expired?

Thank you.

title: Specifying content type in PUT requests?
description:
I'm probably doing something wrong here, but it's not clear how I specify content requests in PUT.
I'm trying to access the [Figshare API](http://api.figshare.com/) with httr.  

Authentication with httr and oauth 1 seems to work fine: 

``` r
figshare_auth <-  function(cKey = getOption("FigshareKey", stop("Missing Figshare consumer key")),
       cSecret = getOption("FigsharePrivateKey", stop("Missing Figshare app secret")),
       token = getOption("FigshareToken", stop("Missing Figshare token")),
       token_secret = getOption("FigsharePrivateToken", stop("Missing Figshare Secret Token"))){
  require(httr)
  myapp <- oauth_app("rfigshare", key = cKey, secret=cSecret)
  sig <-  httr:::sign_ouath1.0(myapp, token = token, token_secret = token_secret) 
  } 

session <- figshare_auth()
```

And most of the basic GET commands work.  But I try to a post method and get:

``` r

figshare_create <- 
function(title="test", description="description of test", type="dataset", session){
  require(RJSONIO)
  base <- "http://api.figshare.com/v1"
  method <- paste("my_data/articles")
  request <- paste(base, method, sep="/")
  meta <- toJSON(list("title"=title, "description"=description,
                      "type"=type, "Content-Type" = "application/json"))
  POST(request, config=session, body=meta)
}
```

and get the error

``` r
figshare_create(session=session)
```

```
Response [http://api.figshare.com/v1/my_data/articles]
  Status: 401
{"error": "Incorect content_type. Expected application/json, received:"} 
```

The GET -based methods work fine (those calls also require the 'session' variable, but I guess this could still be an authentication issue since they shouldn't actually need to authenticate since those should be public methods)?  

Any ideas?  (I'm building out API in rfigshare package here: https://github.com/ropensci/rfigshare)

title: parsed_content mistakes json for xml b/c of header?
description:
I haven't had this error prior to this with other APIs, but the Springer Journals API for some reason gives something in the header that makes parsed_content think that it is html or perhaps xml that is returned when json is actually returned.  I want JSON output, but I get error when wrapping the below call in parsed_content()

For example

tt <- GET(http://api.springer.com/metadata/json?api_key=2pn639bshyrju39zfewygkgd&q=dna)

Then element 4 in the list gives
tt[4]  

content-type in tt[4] is given as "text/html; charset=utf-8", which is perhaps where the problem is?  

Thanks! Scott

title: POST request to create repo on github
description:
I was trying to extend the github demo to create a repo on `github`. I did the `oauth` dance successfully and was able to execute the GET requests correctly. But when I tried to create a repo on `github`, I failed.

Github documentation says that I need to pass the name of the [repo](http://developer.github.com/v3/repos/) as the **scope**, but  I was unable to figure out where I should pass this. The POST request I sent was

``` R
POST('https://api.github.com/user/repos', github_sig)
```

PS. For some reason `oauth2.0_token` is not exported. Is that intentional?
